2.1.title: Administrative Distance (AD) — Quick Reference
rows: The interface is physically connected — always preferred
Manually configured by admin — almost always preferred over dynamic
Routes learned from external BGP peers (internet routing)
Cisco proprietary — DUAL algorithm, fast convergence
Open standard — link-state, area-based, SPF algorithm
Link-state, used by large ISPs, rarely tested on N+
Distance vector, hop count ≤15, slow convergence — legacy
Routes redistributed INTO EIGRP from another protocol
BGP routes learned from internal BGP peers — least trusted dynamic
Never installed in routing table — effectively blocked
key_points: Lower AD = more trustworthy. Router installs LOWEST AD route.
Static AD=1 almost always beats dynamic protocols (AD 90–200).
Floating static route: set AD > dynamic protocol AD to use as backup only.
Memorise: Connected(0) > Static(1) > eBGP(20) > EIGRP(90) > OSPF(110) > RIP(120) > iBGP(200).
Exam trap: 'Which route is preferred?' — always pick lowest AD.

2.1.title: Routing Protocols — Head-to-Head
rows: Small legacy networks — avoid in production
Internet routing between ASes — THE internet protocol
Service provider networks, rarely in enterprise
key_points: IGP (Interior) = inside one AS: RIP, EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS.
EGP (Exterior) = between ASes: BGP (only one in use today).
OSPF area 0 = backbone area — all other areas must connect to area 0.
BGP uses TCP port 179.
OSPF elects DR/BDR on multi-access segments (Ethernet) to reduce LSA flooding.
EIGRP uses RTP (Reliable Transport Protocol) — not TCP/UDP.

2.1.title: NAT Types — Translation Explained
rows: One-to-one: single private IP ↔ single public IP
Hosting a server — needs consistent public IP
Pool: private IP → one public IP from pool
Multiple clients sharing a pool of public IPs
Many-to-one: all private IPs → one public IP + unique port
Home/office internet access — most common NAT
IPv6-only hosts communicating with IPv4 servers
key_points: PAT (Port Address Translation) = NAT Overload — tracks connections by port number.
Static NAT needed for inbound connections (servers, DMZ hosts).
NAT hides internal addressing — 'inside local' is the private IP.
Inside global = public IP seen by internet. Inside local = private IP on LAN.
NAT breaks end-to-end connectivity (can cause VoIP, VPN, gaming issues).

2.1.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRP)
rows: Hot Standby Router Protocol — most common on Cisco
Gateway Load Balancing Protocol — most advanced, Cisco only
key_points: All FHRPs create a virtual IP + virtual MAC shared by the group.
Clients use the VIRTUAL IP as their default gateway — not a physical router IP.
HSRP: one active, one standby. Election: highest priority wins (default 100); tie → highest IP.
VRRP: same concept as HSRP but RFC standard — compatible with all vendors.
GLBP: one AVG (Active Virtual Gateway) assigns different virtual MACs → true load balancing.
Preemption: when a higher-priority router comes back up, it can reclaim active role (must be enabled in HSRP).

2.2.title: VLAN Fundamentals & 802.1Q Trunking
2.2.body:
A VLAN (Virtual LAN) is a logical segment of a switched network. It creates separate broadcast domains without needing physical separation.

802.1Q TAGGING:
When a frame travels over a trunk link, an 802.1Q tag (4 bytes) is inserted into the Ethernet header:
  • Tag Protocol ID (TPID): 0x8100
  • Priority (PCP): 3 bits (QoS/CoS)
  • Drop Eligible (DEI): 1 bit
  • VLAN ID (VID): 12 bits → supports 4094 VLANs (0 and 4095 reserved)

PORT MODES:
  • Access port: belongs to ONE VLAN, frames are UNTAGGED
  • Trunk port: carries MULTIPLE VLANs, frames are TAGGED (except native VLAN)
  • Native VLAN: the ONE VLAN that is NOT tagged on a trunk (default VLAN 1 — change it for security)
  • Voice VLAN: access port can carry data VLAN + voice VLAN simultaneously (for IP phones)
key_points: VLANs create separate broadcast domains — a broadcast in VLAN 10 doesn't reach VLAN 20.
Trunk ports tag ALL VLANs except the native VLAN — native VLAN frames pass untagged.
Native VLAN mismatch = security risk (VLAN hopping) — always set native VLAN to unused VLAN.
Default VLAN is VLAN 1 — all ports start in VLAN 1; best practice is to NOT use VLAN 1 for data.
Inter-VLAN routing requires either a router (router-on-a-stick) or a Layer 3 switch (SVI).
DTP (Dynamic Trunking Protocol) — Cisco auto-negotiates trunk; disable on access ports (switchport nonegotiate).

2.2.title: STP Port States & Roles (802.1D)
key_points: STP convergence = 30–50 seconds total (Blocking→Listening→Learning→Forwarding).
Mnemonic for states: Blocking Learners Listen First — BLLF, or 'Big Losers Listen Forever'.
PORT ROLES: Root Port (toward root bridge), Designated Port (best port on a segment, forwards), Alternate/Backup (blocked to prevent loops).
ROOT BRIDGE: elected by lowest Bridge ID = Bridge Priority (default 32768) + MAC address. Tie: lower MAC wins.
All ports on Root Bridge = Designated (Forwarding).
PortFast: skips Listening/Learning — use on ACCESS ports only (not trunk). Enables immediately.
BPDU Guard: shuts down a PortFast port if it receives a BPDU (protects against accidental switch connections).

2.2.title: STP Variants & LACP
rows: Original — one spanning tree for all VLANs. Too slow for modern networks.
Rapid STP — same logic, much faster. Backward compatible with 802.1D.
Per-VLAN STP — separate tree per VLAN. Rapid PVST+ uses 802.1w per VLAN.
Maps multiple VLANs to fewer STP instances — scalable in large networks.
Combines multiple physical links into one logical link (EtherChannel/Port-Channel). Active/passive modes.
key_points: RSTP (802.1w) = what you should use today — same concept as STP but < 2 sec convergence.
LACP modes: Active (initiates negotiation) and Passive (responds to negotiation). Active-Active or Active-Passive works; Passive-Passive does NOT.
EtherChannel/Port-Channel: up to 8 active links bundled. STP sees it as ONE logical link — no blocking needed.
LACP vs PAgP: LACP is IEEE standard; PAgP is Cisco proprietary (both do link aggregation).
MSTP groups VLANs into instances — reduces CPU load vs PVST+ in large deployments.

2.2.title: Inter-VLAN Routing Methods
rows: Single trunk link from switch to router; router uses subinterfaces (one per VLAN)
Simple setup; router becomes bottleneck at high traffic
Switch itself routes between VLANs using Switch Virtual Interfaces
Fast (hardware routing); no external router needed; most scalable
Each VLAN has a dedicated router port
Simple but wastes ports; impractical for many VLANs
key_points: SVI (Switched Virtual Interface) = virtual Layer 3 interface on a switch, one per VLAN.
Router-on-a-stick: connect switch trunk port to router → create subinterfaces with 802.1Q encapsulation.
Layer 3 switch is always preferred in enterprise (line-rate routing, no bottleneck).
Default gateway for hosts in each VLAN = IP address of the SVI or router subinterface for that VLAN.
Exam question: 'Host A (VLAN 10) can't reach Host B (VLAN 20)' → usually missing SVI or misconfigured inter-VLAN routing.

2.3.title: 802.11 Wireless Standards — Full Comparison
rows: First 5GHz standard. Less range, no 2.4GHz interference.
First widely adopted. Slow; prone to interference (microwaves, BT).
Backward compatible with 802.11b. Replaced b in most deployments.
MIMO (multiple antennas). Channel bonding to 40 MHz. Dual-band.
MU-MIMO, 80/160 MHz channels, beamforming. Common today.
OFDMA, BSS coloring, TWT (Target Wake Time). Dense environments.
key_points: Memorise: a=5GHz/54M, b=2.4GHz/11M, g=2.4GHz/54M, n=both/600M, ac=5GHz/3.5G, ax=all/9.6G.
802.11ac/Wi-Fi 5 = 5GHz ONLY. Cannot use 2.4GHz band.
Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6GHz band — less congestion, more channels, shorter range.
MIMO (n) = multiple antennas transmit/receive simultaneously on same channel.
MU-MIMO (ac/ax) = Multiple User MIMO — serves multiple clients simultaneously.
OFDMA (ax/Wi-Fi 6) = divides channel into sub-carriers per client — efficient in dense deployments.

2.3.title: Wireless Security — WEP/WPA/WPA2/WPA3
rows: BROKEN — do not use. IV reuse → cracked in minutes.
Current standard — still widely used and secure.
Strongest — SAE resists offline dictionary attacks.
Encrypts open networks without authentication (WPA3 feature).
key_points: WPA2 Personal = PSK (pre-shared key / passphrase). WPA2 Enterprise = 802.1X + RADIUS server.
WPA3 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) replaces PSK — prevents offline brute-force attacks.
WPA2 vulnerability: KRACK attack (Key Reinstallation Attack) — mitigated by patches.
802.1X = port-based access control framework. EAP = Extensible Authentication Protocol (runs over 802.1X).
Common EAP types: EAP-TLS (certificate both sides), PEAP (server cert + MSCHAPv2), EAP-FAST.
Captive portal: redirect unauthenticated users to a login page — common in guest Wi-Fi.

2.3.title: Wireless Channel Planning
2.3.body:
2.4 GHz BAND:
  • 11 channels in North America (14 worldwide)
  • Channels are 22 MHz wide but spaced 5 MHz apart → OVERLAP
  • Non-overlapping channels: 1, 6, 11 (the only three that don't interfere)
  • All APs in the same area should use channels 1, 6, or 11
  • 2.4 GHz has only 3 non-overlapping channels → congested in dense environments

5 GHz BAND:
  • 24+ non-overlapping 20 MHz channels (varies by country/regulatory domain)
  • Channels can be bonded: 40 MHz (2 channels), 80 MHz (4 channels), 160 MHz (8 channels)
  • DFS (Dynamic Frequency Selection): some 5GHz channels require radar detection + avoidance
  • UNII-1 (indoor), UNII-2 (DFS), UNII-3, UNII-4 sub-bands

6 GHz BAND (Wi-Fi 6E):
  • 59 non-overlapping 20 MHz channels
  • Huge capacity improvement — ideal for dense deployments
key_points: 2.4 GHz non-overlapping: 1, 6, 11 — MEMORISE THIS. Only these three can coexist without interference.
5 GHz has 24+ non-overlapping channels — much less congestion than 2.4 GHz.
Co-channel interference: two APs on same channel → contention (worse than adjacent channel).
Adjacent channel interference: partially overlapping channels (e.g., 1 and 3) → noise floor rises.
Cell sizing: turn down AP power to avoid overlap in dense deployments (smaller cells = more APs needed).
Site survey: walk-through to measure signal strength, noise, and interference before deploying APs.

2.3.title: AP Architecture & Antenna Types
rows: Fully self-contained — manages own SSID, security, RF. No controller needed. Hard to manage at scale.
Offloads config and management to WLC (Wireless LAN Controller). Uses CAPWAP tunnel to WLC.
Wireless backhaul to other APs — no wired connection to every AP. Extends coverage where cables can't reach.
Connects two wired LAN segments wirelessly — point-to-point or point-to-multipoint.
Radiates 360° horizontally (like a donut shape). Default for most indoor APs. Lower gain (~2–5 dBi).
Focused beam — high gain in one direction. Used for point-to-point links or specific coverage areas.
Extremely high gain, very narrow beam. Long-distance outdoor point-to-point links (up to miles).
Control and Provisioning of Wireless Access Points — UDP 5246 (control) + 5247 (data). LWAP↔WLC tunnel.
key_points: CAPWAP: lightweight AP tunnels all traffic to WLC. UDP 5246 (control plane) + 5247 (data plane).
WLC (Wireless LAN Controller): centrally manages LWAPs — RF profiles, SSIDs, security, roaming.
Autonomous APs: simple to set up individually; nightmare to manage at scale (each configured separately).
Omnidirectional: good for open office/coverage. Directional: good for hallways, point-to-point outdoor.
EIRP (Effective Isotropic Radiated Power): regulated max transmit power including antenna gain.
SSID can be the same across multiple APs → client roams seamlessly (ESS — Extended Service Set).

2.4.title: Data Center Hierarchy — MDF, IDF & Cabling
2.4.body:
WIRING HIERARCHY (3-tier structured cabling):

  Entrance Facility (EF)
       ↓
  Main Distribution Frame (MDF)
       ↓ (vertical/backbone cabling)
  Intermediate Distribution Frame (IDF) — one per floor / wiring closet
       ↓ (horizontal cabling — max 90m)
  Work Area (end devices)

MDF:
  • Houses core/distribution switches, routers, WAN connections, patch panels
  • Central point for the entire building's network
  • Connects to all IDFs via backbone cabling (fiber between floors)

IDF:
  • Floor-level or zone-level wiring closet
  • Houses access layer switches, patch panels
  • Connected to MDF via riser cables (fiber or Cat6A)
  • Contains: switch(es), patch panel, cable management, UPS

HORIZONTAL CABLING (TIA-568):
  • Max 90m permanent link + 10m for patch cables = 100m total
  • Copper (Cat5e/Cat6/Cat6A) — 1000BASE-T up to 100m
  • Fiber for IDF→MDF runs (exceeds copper limit)
key_points: MDF = building's core network hub. IDF = floor/zone distribution point.
Horizontal cabling limit: 90m permanent link + 10m patch = 100m total (TIA-568).
Backbone/vertical cabling connects MDF to IDFs — typically fiber (exceeds 100m copper limit).
66 block (voice/legacy) vs 110 block (data) vs patch panel (modern) — exam knows all three.
Demarcation point (demarc): where ISP's responsibility ends and customer's begins (usually at entrance facility).
Smart jack (NID/NIU): ISP equipment at demarc — tests circuit from ISP side.

2.4.title: UPS Types & Power Infrastructure
rows: Passes utility power directly; battery + inverter only switch on during outage
Voltage regulator (AVR) adjusts output continuously; battery activates for total failure
Good — handles sags and swells without battery
Always runs through inverter — utility charges battery, inverter powers load 100% of time
Best — clean, regulated, isolated from utility
key_points: Offline UPS: basic and cheap — OK for desktops. NOT suitable for sensitive servers.
Line-Interactive: best value for small server rooms — AVR handles brownouts without depleting battery.
Online (Double Conversion): gold standard for data centers — zero transfer time, cleanest power.
UPS runtime: determined by battery capacity (Ah) vs load (W). More load = shorter runtime.
PDU (Power Distribution Unit): rack-mounted power strip. 'Smart PDU' monitors per-outlet wattage.
Generator: long-term backup power; UPS bridges the gap while generator spins up (~10-30 sec).
Redundant power paths: dual PSUs in servers + separate PDUs on separate UPS/circuits.

2.4.title: Physical Environment & Data Center Standards
2.4.body:
HOT AISLE / COLD AISLE (ASHRAE standard):
  • Server racks arranged in alternating rows facing each other
  • Cold aisle: server fronts face each other ← cold air delivered from floor/CRAC unit
  • Hot aisle: server rears face each other → hot exhaust vented to return/ceiling
  • Prevents hot and cold air from mixing → improves cooling efficiency

RACK UNITS:
  • 1U = 1.75 inches of vertical rack space
  • Standard rack = 42U
  • 'Half-depth' servers: 2-post rack (open frame); full-depth servers need 4-post rack

ENVIRONMENTAL MONITORING:
  • Temperature: ASHRAE A2 class = 10°C–35°C (50°F–95°F) for most IT equipment
  • Humidity: 40–60% RH recommended. Too low → ESD risk. Too high → condensation.
  • Environmental sensors alert on temp/humidity out of range

FIRE SUPPRESSION:
  • NEVER water in a server room — use clean agent suppression
  • FM-200 (HFC-227ea): fast, leaves no residue, safe for occupied rooms
  • Halon: replaced by FM-200 (Halon depletes ozone — banned for new installations)
  • CO₂: effective but displaces oxygen — evacuate before activation

PHYSICAL SECURITY:
  • Mantrap (airlock): two doors — only one opens at a time
  • Biometric + badge: multi-factor physical access
  • CCTV: surveillance logging for audit trails
key_points: Hot/cold aisle containment: alternating front-to-front and back-to-back rack rows.
1U = 1.75 inches. Standard rack = 42U (~7 feet). Know this for port density questions.
ASHRAE A2 temperature range: 10°C–35°C — most servers today can tolerate this range.
FM-200 = safe clean agent for occupied server rooms. CO₂ requires evacuation.
ESD (Electrostatic Discharge): risk when humidity too low — ground strap, anti-static mats.
Raised floor: allows underfloor cable management and cold air distribution from CRAC units.
